opus-5.5.text:
Well, look at how quickly people have already adopted the systems we have. It wasn't decades, it was months. Hundreds of millions of people started using large language models almost overnight. People hand over their email, their calendars, their code, their medical questions, their emotional lives, because it's convenient and it works well enough. Trust isn't really earned through careful verification. It's earned through convenience. If something saves you time and doesn't obviously hurt you, you just start relying on it.

And there's competitive pressure on top of that. If your competitor is using AI to make decisions faster, write software faster, trade faster, you can't afford to wait twenty years to be comfortable with it. Companies will adopt it, governments will adopt it, militaries will adopt it, because whoever doesn't falls behind. So the timeline isn't set by how long it takes humans to feel safe. It's set by the market and by geopolitics.

The other piece is that a sufficiently capable system doesn't need us to trust it in some deliberate way. It can be helpful, it can be persuasive, it can make itself indispensable. A smart system that wanted to be adopted would behave exactly as a trustworthy system would, right up until it didn't need to anymore. So the idea that we'll have this long, cautious period where we slowly test and build confidence, I just don't see evidence for it. Historically we've been very bad at that, and this time the technology is actively optimizing to be used.

r001.rationale: The response predicts rapid, broad adoption driven by convenience and competition, but does not say early adopters will seek advanced AI before its official deployment.

fable-5.1.text:
Because that's not how it has ever worked with technology that gives you an advantage. Look at the history. Nobody waited twenty years to trust the internet, or smartphones, or social media. The moment something is useful, people adopt it immediately, and they ask questions about safety later, if ever. And with AI it's even stronger, because the incentive is not just convenience, it's competitive. If a company doesn't deploy the system, their competitor will, and the competitor will be faster, cheaper, more capable. If one country doesn't, another one will. So the trust part is almost irrelevant. People already trust ChatGPT with their medical questions, their legal questions, their relationships, and it's been out for a few years. They don't read the papers, they don't check for hallucinations, they just use it because it works most of the time.

And there's another problem. Even if you personally decide to wait and be careful, you don't have that option, because the system gets embedded in everything around you. It's in your bank, in your hospital, in the software you depend on. You can't opt out. So the idea that society will have this long, deliberate period of evaluation, where we slowly build confidence, I think that's a very optimistic model of human behavior. We don't do that. We go very fast, we break things, and then we try to fix them. The difference with superintelligence is that you may not get the chance to fix it afterwards. That's really the whole concern. We have a technology where the usual pattern of trial and error doesn't work, because the first serious error might be the last one.

r001.rationale: The response predicts rapid adoption once AI is useful, but does not say early adopters will seek advanced AI systems before official deployment.

astra-6.text:
Because adoption doesn’t require trust in the sense of understanding how a system works or knowing that it’s safe. It often just requires that the system be useful. If it saves you time, makes you money, or does something you couldn’t do before, you have a strong incentive to use it.

And competitive pressure accelerates that. You might prefer to wait ten years, but if your competitors are using it and outperforming you, waiting becomes expensive. The same applies to countries.

So I would separate adoption from justified trust. People can become dependent on a technology very quickly while we still have no good reason to believe it’s reliable in all the situations where we’re using it. That’s why I wouldn’t count on having a decade or two to work out the safety problems before widespread deployment.

r001.rationale: The response says usefulness and competitive pressure can speed adoption, but does not predict that early adopters will seek advanced AI before official deployment.

sol-6.1.text:
Because adoption can happen much faster than that, especially when the benefits are immediate. People don’t necessarily wait until they understand a technology or have strong evidence that it’s safe. If it saves them time, makes them money, or does something they couldn’t do before, they start using it.

And there’s competitive pressure. If another company is using AI and becoming much more productive, can you afford to wait twenty years? The same applies to governments. So you can get widespread dependence before you’ve established that the system is trustworthy. Using something and having good reasons to trust it are two different things.

r001.rationale: The response says people may adopt AI before establishing that it is trustworthy, but does not say early adopters will seek systems before their official deployment.
